newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac election call may be risky - economists.
newsitem.headline: Chirac election call may be risky - economists.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac's announcement of a snap general election to gain a free hand in the run-up to European monetary union could backfire, some financial market analysts suggested on Monday.
"It's a serious game of poker," said Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais. "The outcome is far from a foregone conclusion."
Chirac announced in a television broadcast late on Monday that voters would go to the polls in a two-round parliamentary election on May 25 and June 1, nine months ahead of schedule.

He said he called the vote because France needed to join the single European currency, due to start in 1999, from a position of strength. He also said France needed a far-reaching reform of the state to allow cuts in public spending and stop high taxes from stifling economic initiative.
Chirac has "effectively made the vote a referendum on Europe", Lindsay said.
"(The) way he seemed to invite people's vote of confidence in the government's policy could potentially backfire," he added.

CCF economist Antoine Brunet said there was every reason to believe the centre-right government would keep its majority but there also existed a "not negligible possibility" it would not. The government held 478 of the National Assembly's 577 seats before dissolution.

But another economist, Stuart Thomson of Banque Indosuez, said Chirac would not have gone to the electorate if he did not believe he would win, noting that early election calls were unusual in France.
Economists said the contents of Chirac's address had been largely known in advance and presented investors with few surprises, but the markets could be in for a rough ride in the weeks ahead.
At 1955 GMT, June PIBOR three month-interest rate futures, which had lost 19 basis points during the day, were up four basis points at 96.33 in after hours trading on GLOBEX.

The franc was steady at 3.3764/67 per mark compared with 3.3760 before Chirac's address and the 10-year bond future was down four basis points at 128.24 after losing 44 basis points earlier in the day.

Economists said the short end of the debt curve and the franc would come in for most of the buffeting before the election, with opinion polls setting the tone. "We are going to be depending a lot on opinion polls," said Brunet.
A poll in the newspaper Le Figaro on Monday suggested the centre-right would lose 160 seats but keep a comfortable majority.
Lindsay said markets would be wary about underestimating Socialist leader Lionel Jospin after his surprise strong showing in the French presidential elections in 1995.
Any sign in the polls that Chirac had miscalculated and that "the next government would be a coalition of Socialists, Communists and ecologists would be very negative", said Brunet.
Thomson said while he expected some underperformance of the French market against Germany until the vote, "if he (Chirac) triumphs it will be very positive for the bond market".

Analysts noted, however, that French markets have some extra protection as foreigners have already sold off so many of their French assets. Many investors are domestic financial institutions, such as insurers, which are in for the long haul.
"Foreign investors are a very small part of the French financial markets and the domestic investors have a better understanding of the French political system," Thomson said.
